title: Meaning, even here
hookLine: Viktor Frankl, a psychiatrist who was held in the Nazi camps, argued meaning can be found even in suffering (Man's Search for Meaning)

lines: WHAT IF YOU HAD DIED FIRST?
cards: An older doctor comes to see a psychiatrist. His wife has died, and he can't get out from under the grief. He loved her above everything, he says.

The psychiatrist doesn't offer advice. He asks a question instead: what would have happened if you had died first, and she had been left to go on without you? The man answers: for her, that would have been terrible.
How she would have suffered. The psychiatrist was Viktor Frankl, and he tells this story in Man's Search for Meaning.

teach.b: First, the turn. Frankl answers, in paraphrase: you see, she was spared that suffering, and it was you who spared her, at the price of surviving her and mourning her. The man says nothing more.
He shakes Frankl's hand and leaves. Nothing about the loss has changed; the grief is still there. But, Frankl writes, it now had a meaning: a sacrifice made for her.

He had been a prisoner in the Nazi camps, Auschwitz among them, and the first part of his book is his plain account of that time. Not a hero story: hunger, cold, and what he saw people do, the worst and the best.

teach.h: DEED, LOVE, AND THE STANCE YOU TAKE.
teach.b: Frankl names ways a person finds meaning: by doing a deed or making something, by loving someone or experiencing something, and, when suffering can't be avoided, by the stance a person takes toward it.

teach.h: IF YOU CAN END IT, END IT.

teach.b: Suffering isn't needed for meaning, he says. If suffering can be avoided, the meaningful thing is to remove it, whether the cause or the pain.
Choosing pain you don't have to bear isn't heroic, in his words; it's just needless. Meaning is not the reason something hard happens. It's something a person can still find, or make, inside it.
And no one gets to hand it to someone else. The doctor found his own, in answer to a question.

how: Frankl's approach, which he called logotherapy, is taught in some counseling and psychotherapy training, and his book is read by people facing grief, illness and loss.

o: a reward handed out for suffering well
the hidden reason behind every hard event
what you can still find in how you bear it

games.q: inside Frankl's question — tap the pairs.
p: what if you had died first?
the meaning he found in his grief

s: Frankl says suffering is necessary to find meaning
he says if suffering can be avoided, the meaningful thing is to end it.
Frankl's question didn't take away the doctor's grief
the loss stayed; what changed is that it had a meaning.
Frankl writes his time in the camps as a hero story
he writes plainly about hunger, cold, and the worst and the best he saw.

games.q: you're Frankl. an older doctor sits across from you, crushed by grief for his wife. what do you say?
o: what if you had died first?
games.why: Frankl asks a question. the man sees that his wife was spared the grief he now carries, and he leaves with the same loss and a meaning for it.

practice: Choose one hard thing in your life you can hold, a caregiving season, a job you can't leave yet, a loss, and gently ask it Frankl's kind of question: who is this for, and what could it make possible, even something small?
If an answer comes, let it be modest; if none comes, that's allowed, and the question can wait.

wordCard.voice: Meaning. For Frankl, what a person can still find in deeds, in love, and, when suffering can't be avoided, in how they bear it. Not the reason for the pain. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek. Frankl named his approach logotherapy and took logos in the sense of meaning.

carryVoice: Your line: a sacrifice made for her. The grief stayed; what changed was its meaning. That's day seven hundred thirty-two.
